quality_flags: The abstract reports 705 patients, whereas the Results section reports 706 patients.
metadata.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates obliteration, symptom outcomes, hemorrhage, and permanent neurological deficits after stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs). It presents practice recommendations for selecting patients, planning SRS, and assessing obliteration during follow-up. It also discusses how fistula location, grade, previous hemorrhage, and embolization relate to treatment decisions and outcomes.

target_population: Patients with dAVFs treated with SRS
Patients with complex dAVFs unlikely to achieve CO with embolization alone
Patients with dAVFs and refractory symptoms after embolization without CO
Patients with high-risk NCS dAVFs or symptomatic CS dAVFs who cannot undergo or decline embolization and microsurgery

toxicities.incidence: Across 14 studies involving 605 patients, the pooled rate at final clinical follow-up was 1.1% (95% CI 0.6%-1.6%).
prevention: Consider prior hemorrhage when counseling patients about hemorrhage risk after SRS.

toxicities.incidence: Across 12 studies involving 283 patients, the pooled rate at final clinical follow-up was 1.3% (95% CI 0.8%-1.8%).
O’Leary et al reported 1/14 patients with clinical follow-up (7.2%).

therapies_index.name: SRS
approved_indications: Complex dAVFs for which embolization alone is unlikely to achieve CO, particularly when surgery is unsuitable.
dAVFs with persistent symptoms and no CO after embolization.
High-risk NCS dAVFs, including Borden type II or III or lesions with previous hemorrhage, and symptomatic CS dAVFs when embolization and microsurgery are unsuitable or refused.
Definitive, adjuvant, or salvage treatment, according to fistula size and proximity to at-risk normal structures.
therapies_index.administration: Single-fraction SRS is recommended with contemporary MPDs of approximately 17-25 Gy, subject to fistula size and surrounding tissue tolerances. The target generally includes the fistula without the feeding artery or draining vein; a 1-mm PTV expansion may be used when needed.
key_toxicities: PNDs after SRS; reported manifestations include reduced visual acuity and permanent hearing loss.
monitoring: Obtain MRI/A, or CT/A if MRI is not feasible, every 6 months after SRS until obliteration is suspected.
Use cerebral angiography to confirm suspected CO when feasible.

therapies_index.name: GK-SRS
approved_indications: Treatment of dAVFs in the cited clinical series.
therapies_index.administration: The cited series generally administered GK-SRS in a single fraction; prescription doses varied between studies.

therapies_index.name: LINAC-SRS
approved_indications: Treatment of NCS dAVFs in the series by Gross et al.
therapies_index.administration: The series used single-fraction LINAC-SRS with an MPD of 17.7 Gy (15-20 Gy).

therapies_index.name: endovascular embolization
approved_indications: First-line treatment for high-grade and/or symptomatic dAVFs.
Treatment before SRS when embolization alone is unlikely to achieve CO.
key_toxicities: New neurological deficits attributed to embolization in the series by Pollock et al.
Potential obscuring of the dAVF on stereotactic imaging when embolization precedes SRS.

therapies_index.name: microsurgical ligation
approved_indications: An alternative treatment for dAVFs, either alone or with embolization.

therapies_index.name: embolization and SRS
approved_indications: Clinically aggressive dAVFs or fistulas refractory to embolization when combined treatment is feasible.
Complex fistulas unlikely to achieve CO with embolization alone, or fistulas without CO and/or with recurrent symptoms after embolization.
therapies_index.administration: When embolization is planned before SRS, acquire SRS planning images after embolization to delineate the residual fistula.

therapies_index.name: conservative management
approved_indications: An initial option for CS dAVFs and low-grade intracranial dAVFs.
monitoring: Close clinical and radiographic follow-up may be indicated because CVD can develop.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose fistulas are suitable for initial conservative management.
decision_rules: Initial observation and conservative management are viable for CS dAVFs.
If symptoms remain refractory or progress, definitive treatment is recommended.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation and conservative management
recommended_regimens.summary: An acceptable initial approach, with clinical and radiographic surveillance considered because CVD can develop.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: CS dAVFs may cause refractory ophthalmological symptoms and potentially progressive vision loss.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with low-grade fistulas at low risk of serious sequelae.
decision_rules: Initial observation and conservative management are viable.
Definitive treatment is recommended if symptoms remain refractory or progress after conservative management.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation and conservative management
recommended_regimens.summary: An acceptable initial approach for a low-risk fistula; close clinical and radiographic follow-up may be indicated because CVD can develop.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients undergoing initial treatment for high-grade and/or symptomatic fistulas.
decision_rules: Embolization is recommended as the first-line treatment.
For complex fistulas unlikely to reach CO with embolization alone, consider the pathway combining embolization with SRS.
Microsurgical ligation is an alternative used alone or with embolization.

recommended_regimens.name: Endovascular embolization
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommended initial treatment for high-grade and/or symptomatic dAVFs.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document reports a CO rate between 70% and 90% for endovascular embolization.

alternative_regimens.name: Microsurgical ligation
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative that may be performed alone or combined with embolization.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Embolization, with or without microsurgical ligation, may fail to achieve CO or durable cure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with Borden type II or III fistulas or previous hemorrhage.
decision_rules: Definitive treatment is recommended because high-grade NCS dAVFs carry risks of morbidity and mortality.
Use embolization as first-line treatment when feasible.
SRS is recommended when neither embolization nor microsurgical ligation is feasible, or when the patient has refused both.

recommended_regimens.name: Endovascular embolization
recommended_regimens.summary: Recommended first-line intervention when feasible for a high-risk fistula.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document reports a CO rate between 70% and 90% for endovascular embolization.

alternative_regimens.name: SRS
alternative_regimens.summary: Recommended when embolization and microsurgical ligation are infeasible or both have been refused; single-fraction treatment depends on fistula size and nearby structures at risk.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Borden type II or III or previous hemorrhage, together with inability to undergo or refusal of both embolization and microsurgery.

alternative_regimens.name: Microsurgical ligation
alternative_regimens.summary: An alternative to embolization, either alone or combined with it.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 6 months after SRS until obliteration is suspected
response_assessment.method: Serial MRI/A, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible

response_assessment.interpretation: Confirm CO definitively; if angiography cannot be performed, MRI/A or CT/CTA may establish CO with a high degree of confidence.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: When SRS is used, patients should be counseled that CO may be delayed. Previous hemorrhage should inform counseling about hemorrhage risk after SRS.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with complex fistulas scheduled for embolization who have a high risk of not achieving CO with embolization alone.
decision_rules: Combined embolization and SRS is recommended when feasible for clinically aggressive dAVFs or fistulas refractory to embolization, to maximize the likelihood of symptom cure.
When embolization precedes SRS, obtain planning images after embolization so the residual fistula can be delineated.
Select single-fraction SRS according to fistula size and proximity to normal structures at risk.

recommended_regimens.name: Embolization and SRS
recommended_regimens.summary: Use embolization with SRS for a complex or clinically aggressive fistula when combined treatment is feasible. The document recommends single-fraction SRS in appropriate definitive or adjuvant settings, with contemporary MPDs of approximately 17-25 Gy and a 1-mm PTV expansion if needed.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the pooled analysis after SRS, CO was 68.6% (95% CI 60.7%-76.5%), symptom improvement was 97.2% (95% CI 93.2%-100%), and symptom cure was 78.8% (95% CI 69.3%-88.2%). Previous embolization was associated with higher symptom cure rates (P = .01); these pooled rates are not comparative estimates for the combined regimen.

response_assessment.method: Pretreatment cerebral angiography and thin-slice (1 mm or less) MRI/A with T1 pregadolinium and postgadolinium sequences, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible
response_assessment.interpretation: Delineate the residual fistula for SRS; MRI is particularly recommended, when feasible, for targets near the brain stem, cochlea, or optic apparatus.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 6 months after SRS until obliteration is suspected
response_assessment.method: Serial MRI/A, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible

response_assessment.interpretation: Confirm CO definitively; if angiography cannot be performed, MRI/A or CT/CTA may establish CO with a high degree of confidence.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Embolization may make subsequent SRS safer by reducing fistula size, but may also obscure the target on stereotactic imaging. The SRS target generally includes the fistula without its feeding artery or draining vein. Counsel patients that CO after SRS may be delayed. The analysis could not compare SRS alone directly with multimodality treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with previous embolization without CO and/or recurrent symptoms, or with previous hemorrhage before definitive treatment, particularly when microsurgical ligation is infeasible or refused.
decision_rules: SRS is recommended as an adjuvant or salvage option after embolization fails to produce CO and/or symptoms recur.
SRS is also recommended in the described complex-fistula setting for patients with hemorrhage before definitive treatment, especially if microsurgical ligation cannot be performed or is refused.
Select single-fraction SRS according to fistula size and surrounding normal-tissue tolerances.

recommended_regimens.name: SRS
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjuvant or salvage treatment after unsuccessful embolization, or in the described setting of previous hemorrhage. The document recommends single-fraction SRS with contemporary MPDs of approximately 17-25 Gy, depending on fistula size and normal-tissue tolerances, and a 1-mm PTV expansion if needed.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Across the pooled SRS studies, CO was 68.6% (95% CI 60.7%-76.5%), symptom improvement was 97.2% (95% CI 93.2%-100%), and symptom cure was 78.8% (95% CI 69.3%-88.2%). These are overall SRS estimates, not salvage-specific rates.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before SRS, after any planned embolization
response_assessment.method: Cerebral angiography and thin-slice (1 mm or less) MRI/A with T1 pregadolinium and postgadolinium sequences, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible
response_assessment.interpretation: Define the residual fistula and avoid critical structures; MRI is particularly recommended when feasible for targets near the brain stem, cochlea, or optic apparatus.

response_assessment.timepoint: Every 6 months after SRS until obliteration is suspected
response_assessment.method: Serial MRI/A, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible

response_assessment.interpretation: Confirm CO definitively; if angiography cannot be performed, MRI/A or CT/CTA may establish CO with a high degree of confidence.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The SRS target generally comprises the fistula, not its feeding artery or draining vein. Counsel patients that CO may be delayed; previous hemorrhage should be considered when discussing post-SRS hemorrhage risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with symptomatic CS dAVFs whose symptoms remain refractory or progress after initial conservative management, including those unable to undergo or refusing both embolization and microsurgery.

SRS is recommended when embolization and microsurgical ligation are infeasible or both have been refused.

alternative_regimens.summary: Recommended for symptomatic CS dAVFs when embolization and microsurgery cannot be performed or both have been refused. Single-fraction treatment depends on fistula size and proximity to structures at risk.

response_assessment.method: Serial MRI/A, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible

response_assessment.interpretation: Confirm CO definitively; if angiography cannot be performed, MRI/A or CT/CTA may establish CO with a high degree of confidence.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If SRS is used, counsel patients that CO may be delayed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with refractory or progressive symptoms after initial conservative management.
decision_rules: Definitive treatment is recommended if symptoms remain refractory or progress after conservative management.
Embolization is recommended as first-line treatment for symptomatic dAVFs.

recommended_regimens.name: Endovascular embolization
recommended_regimens.summary: First-line intervention for a symptomatic fistula requiring definitive treatment.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document reports a CO rate between 70% and 90% for endovascular embolization.

Definitive treatment is recommended for high-grade NCS dAVFs, including Borden types II and III.

Embolization is recommended as first-line treatment for high-grade and/or symptomatic dAVFs.
Consider SRS for complex dAVFs when embolization is planned but is unlikely to achieve CO on its own.

conditions.name: dAVFs
conditions.description: Uncommon arteriovenous shunts connecting meningeal arteries to venous sinuses or meningeal or cortical veins. Their clinical course depends on venous drainage.
conditions.epidemiology: They account for approximately 10% to 15% of intracranial vascular malformations.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations may include neurological symptoms related to venous congestion, ophthalmological complaints, nonhemorrhagic neurological deficits, and intracranial hemorrhage; presentation varies with fistula location and drainage pattern.

subtypes.name: CS dAVFs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Generally have a more benign course than NCS dAVFs, but ophthalmological symptoms may be persistent and vision may deteriorate.

subtypes.name: NCS dAVFs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Location outside the cavernous sinus is associated with lower complete obliteration and symptom-cure rates after SRS.

subtypes.name: low-grade intracranial dAVFs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Initial observation and conservative management are viable options, although development of CVD remains a small risk.

subtypes.name: high-grade NCS dAVFs
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Direct CVD characterizes aggressive fistulas; Borden types II and III are identified as high-grade.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the diagnosis of dAVFs and assess symptoms and venous drainage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clinical symptoms, CVD, and drainage pattern help distinguish less aggressive from more aggressive fistulas.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Define the fistula for SRS planning and establish whether complete obliteration has occurred.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before SRS and when serial imaging suggests obliteration.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Absence of a residual fistula supports complete obliteration.

diagnostic_workup.test: Thin-slice MRI/A with T1 pregadolinium and postgadolinium sequences
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Delineate the residual fistula and identify nearby structures at risk during SRS planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before SRS; MRI is particularly recommended when the target is near the brain stem, cochlea, or optic apparatus. If embolization precedes SRS, obtain planning images after embolization.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide imaging for SRS planning or follow-up when MRI/A is not feasible.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When MRI/A cannot be performed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: May be used to assess complete obliteration if confirmatory cerebral angiography cannot be performed.

definitions.description: The document reports this category but does not specify its drainage-based definition.
Identified as a high-grade category; its specific drainage-based definition is not provided.
Identified as a high-grade category; its specific drainage-based definition is not provided.

staging.additional_rules: Borden and Cognard classifications describe clinical and radiographic features of NCS dAVFs, including venous drainage patterns. The document does not provide definitions for Cognard categories.

prognostic_tools.name: Borden

risk_groups.expected_outcome: Higher grade was associated with a lower rate of symptom cure after SRS (P = .04).

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The classification helps characterize the risk associated with NCS dAVFs; the document does not specify definitions for individual types.

prognostic_tools.name: Cognard
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Mentioned as a classification used to distinguish less aggressive from more aggressive NCS dAVFs; category definitions are not supplied.

follow_up.schedule: After SRS, obtain serial imaging every 6 months until obliteration is suspected. Close clinical and radiographic follow-up may be indicated during conservative management because CVD can develop.
recommended_tests: MRI/A every 6 months after SRS, or CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible
Cerebral angiography to confirm suspected complete obliteration
MRI/A or CT/CTA to assess obliteration when confirmatory cerebral angiography cannot be performed
long_term_effects: Monitor for post-SRS hemorrhage and permanent neurological deficits; visual-acuity decline and hearing loss were reported in earlier studies.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should be informed that complete obliteration may occur only after a delay following SRS.

conditions.name: CS dAVFs
conditions.description: Fistulas involving the cavernous sinus that generally follow a more benign course than aggressive NCS dAVFs.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause multiple persistent ophthalmological complaints and progressive vision loss associated with increased intraocular pressure and/or reduced ocular perfusion.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: Persistent or progressive symptoms after conservative management warrant definitive treatment; SRS is an option when embolization and microsurgery are unsuitable or declined.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Guide SRS planning and confirm suspected complete obliteration.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Delineate the target and nearby structures at risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Serve as an imaging alternative for planning or surveillance.

artifacts.title: TABLE 2. Practice Guidelines and Recommendations on Role of SRS for dAVFs

rows: (a) Consider SRS for complex dAVFs when embolization is planned but is unlikely to achieve CO alone. (b) Consider SRS when prior embolization has not achieved CO and symptoms remain refractory. (c) Consider SRS for high-risk NCS dAVFs (Borden type II or III, or previous hemorrhage) or symptomatic CS dAVFs when patients cannot undergo or decline both embolization and microsurgery.

(a) Obtain cerebral angiography and thin-slice (1 mm or less) MRI/A before treatment, using T1 sequences before and after gadolinium; use CT/A if MRI/A is not feasible. (b) MRI is particularly recommended, when feasible, for targets near the brain stem, cochlea or optic apparatus. (c) When embolization precedes SRS, acquire planning images after embolization to define the remaining fistula more clearly. (d) Single-fraction SRS is recommended in definitive, adjuvant or salvage settings according to fistula size and proximity to at-risk normal structures; add a 1-mm PTV expansion when needed.

(a) Follow patients with serial MRI/As, or CT/A if these are not feasible, every 6 months after SRS until obliteration is suspected. (b) When serial imaging suggests CO, a cerebral angiogram is recommended for definitive confirmation.

document_sections.heading: BACKGROUND
document_sections.content: Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is used for dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs) to obtain complete obliteration (CO), reduce subsequent hemorrhage risk, and relieve neurological symptoms.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVE
document_sections.content: The review evaluates outcomes following SRS for dAVFs and develops practice recommendations.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The review followed PICOS, PRISMA, and MOOSE methods. Eligible patients had dAVFs treated with SRS and available information on at least one study outcome. Outcomes included CO, symptom improvement or cure, hemorrhage after SRS, and permanent neurological deficits (PNDs). Pooled outcome estimates used weighted random-effects analyses with the DerSimonian and Laird method. Weighted mixed-effects regression examined relationships between patient or lesion features and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The abstract reports 21 published studies comprising 705 patients with 721 dAVFs treated with SRS. Pooled CO was 68.6% (95% CI 60.7%-76.5%); symptom improvement was 97.2% (95% CI 93.2%-100%), and symptom cure was 78.8% (95% CI 69.3%-88.2%). Estimated hemorrhage after SRS was 1.1% (95% CI 0.6%-1.6%), and estimated PND incidence was 1.3% (95% CI 0.8%-1.8%). Noncavernous sinus (NCS) dAVFs were associated with less CO (P = .03) and less symptom cure (P = .001). Higher grade was associated with less symptom cure (P = .04), whereas prior embolization was associated with more symptom cure (P = .01).

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSION
document_sections.content: Most patients with dAVFs achieved CO after SRS; symptom improvement was frequent, and toxicity was limited. NCS location and higher grade were associated with poorer symptom cure. The authors recommend combining embolization with SRS when feasible for clinically aggressive dAVFs or fistulas refractory to embolization, to increase the likelihood of symptom cure.

document_sections.heading: Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Dural Arteriovenous Fistulas: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis and International Stereotactic Radiosurgery Society Practice Guidelines
document_sections.content: dAVFs are uncommon arteriovenous shunts connecting meningeal arteries to venous sinuses or meningeal or cortical veins. They account for approximately 10% to 15% of intracranial vascular malformations. Venous drainage determines much of their natural history. Cavernous sinus (CS) dAVFs generally have a more benign course but can cause persistent ophthalmological symptoms and progressive visual loss through increased intraocular pressure and/or reduced ocular perfusion. NCS dAVFs with direct cortical venous drainage (CVD), described as high-grade fistulas, are more aggressive. If untreated, they are associated with nonhemorrhagic neurological deficits and intracranial hemorrhage, with mortality rates of up to 35% and 45%, respectively. Treatment primarily seeks to prevent initial or recurrent hemorrhage and relieve neurological symptoms caused by venous congestion. Available interventions include endovascular embolization, microsurgical ligation, and SRS. Embolization is the most common approach and has a reported CO rate between 70% and 90%. Microsurgical ligation can be used alone or with embolization. For complex dAVFs unlikely to be obliterated by embolization alone in patients who are not suitable surgical candidates, SRS offers a minimally invasive option with low complication rates. Published SRS series have been retrospective, with differing follow-up periods and outcome reporting. This review therefore assesses the published evidence on SRS outcomes and presents practice guidance on behalf of the International Stereotactic Radiosurgery Society (ISRS).

document_sections.heading: Study Selection
document_sections.content: PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published through May 1, 2021. Search terms, combined with AND/OR, covered radiosurgery, stereotactic treatment, dural arteriovenous fistula, dAVF, SRS, obliteration, symptom cure or improvement, hemorrhage, neurologic deficit, cortical venous drainage, CVD, low-flow, high-flow, GammaKnife, LINAC, and CyberKnife. PICOS defined initial eligibility; the review also followed PRISMA and MOOSE guidance. Reference lists of included studies were examined. The study had no registered review protocol number. Inclusion required a clinical or radiographic diagnosis of CS or NCS dAVF treated with SRS and data for at least one outcome. Exclusions were absence of outcome data, ≤5 SRS-treated dAVFs, median follow-up of <1 year, overlapping cohorts when a larger series was available, nonhuman studies, publications in languages other than English, and reports available only as abstracts. Single-institution reports were preferred when needed to reduce possible patient duplication.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction
document_sections.content: The first author, R. S., performed the literature search and extracted CO, symptom cure and improvement, hemorrhage after SRS, and PND rates. Extracted characteristics included prescription dose, target volume, previous embolization or surgical ligation, age, Borden class, CVD, and the proportions of CS and NCS dAVFs. CO meant no residual fistula on post-SRS imaging, assessed by angiography, MRI/magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), or computerized tomography/angiography (CT/A) according to institutional practice. Symptom improvement included partial improvement or complete resolution of presenting symptoms by the last clinical follow-up. Symptom cure required complete resolution of those symptoms by that follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Primary and Secondary Outcomes
document_sections.content: Primary outcomes were CO and symptom cure or improvement after SRS at final follow-up. Secondary outcomes were hemorrhage after SRS and PNDs due to treatment toxicity or treatment failure at final follow-up. Most studies assessed CO by angiography, while some assessed possible CO through noninvasive CT/CTA or MRI/A. Radiographic assessment was generally performed 2 to 3 years after SRS. The interval to final clinical assessment of symptoms, hemorrhage, and PNDs differed across studies.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Analyses used Meta-Analysis for R (metafor) package version 2.0-0 in R Studio Version 1.1.383. Study-level outcome proportions and variances were calculated with the DerSimonian and Laird method. Sample-size-weighted random-effects models generated pooled estimates and forest plots. Heterogeneity was evaluated with I2 and the Cochran Q-test; it was classified as significant when both I2 > 50% and P-value < .10 applied. Egger’s test assessed publication bias. A two-tailed t-test result of P ≤ .05 defined statistical significance. For outcomes with significant heterogeneity, mixed-effects meta-regression using ordinary least squares examined median prescription dose (MPD), median target volume, prior embolization or surgery, CVD, the proportions of NCS and CS dAVFs, high-grade dAVFs defined as Borden grades II and III, and hemorrhage before SRS. Regression weights reflected each study’s patients or lesions divided by the corresponding total across studies in that regression.

document_sections.heading: Ethics
document_sections.content: The authors state that study procedures followed the applicable institutional or regional human-experimentation ethics standards or the World Medical Association’s Helsinki Declaration (1964, amended in 1975, 1983, 1989, 1996, and 2000).

document_sections.heading: Patient, Study, and Lesion Characteristics
document_sections.content: In the main results, 21 eligible published studies included 706 patients and 721 SRS-treated dAVFs; the abstract instead reports 705 patients. Treatment occurred between 1994 and 2021 in the United States, Sweden, Canada, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Spain, and India. Table 1 presents study-level outcomes and characteristics, including age, follow-up, prior treatment, hemorrhage, CVD, volume, Borden class, and dose. Cohort median age was 59 years (range: 13-90 years). Median/mean treatment volume was 2.45 cc (range: 0.04-37.5 cc). MPD was 19.1 Gy (range: 13-33 Gy), with a median isodose of 50%. Median clinical follow-up across studies was 2.75 years (range: 3.8 months-15.5 years). Across studies, prior surgery ranged from 0% to 22.2%, prior embolization from 0% to 71.4%, and CVD from 0% to 72.3%.

document_sections.heading: Complete Obliteration, Symptom Cure, and Symptom Improvement Rates
document_sections.content: CO data came from 19 studies and 688 lesions. At final radiological follow-up, pooled CO after SRS was 68.6% (95% CI 60.7%-76.5%). Heterogeneity was significant. A greater proportion of NCS dAVFs was associated with lower CO; differences in MPD, nidus size, earlier surgery or embolization, CVD, higher grade, and hemorrhage before SRS did not explain the heterogeneity. Egger’s test for CO was nonsignificant. Symptom improvement data came from 13 studies and 452 patients. At final clinical follow-up, pooled improvement was 97.2% (95% CI 93.2%-100%). Heterogeneity was significant and was not explained by MPD, nidus size, NCS proportion, higher grade, previous surgery or embolization, CVD, or hemorrhage before SRS. Egger’s test for improvement was nonsignificant. Symptom cure data came from 8 studies and 390 patients. At final clinical follow-up, pooled cure was 78.8% (95% CI 69.3%88.2%). Heterogeneity was significant. Higher grade (P = .04) and a greater NCS proportion (P = .001) were associated with less symptom cure; embolization before SRS was associated with more symptom cure (P = .01). Hemorrhage before SRS, nidus size, MPD, prior surgery, and CVD did not explain further heterogeneity. Egger’s test for cure was nonsignificant.

document_sections.heading: Post-SRS Hemorrhage and Permanent Neurological Deficit Rates
document_sections.content: PND data came from 12 studies and 283 patients. At final clinical follow-up, pooled PND incidence after SRS was 1.3% (95% CI 0.8%-1.8%). Between-study heterogeneity was not significant. Prior surgery or embolization, MPD, nidus size, NCS proportion, higher grade, previous hemorrhage, and CVD were not associated with PND incidence. Egger’s test was nonsignificant. Hemorrhage after SRS was reported by 14 studies involving 605 patients. Its pooled incidence at final clinical follow-up was 1.1% (95% CI 0.6%-1.6%), without significant heterogeneity. Previous hemorrhage correlated positively with hemorrhage after SRS (P = .007). MPD, earlier surgery or embolization, nidus size, NCS proportion, and higher grade were not associated with hemorrhage after SRS. Egger’s test for this outcome was nonsignificant.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: dAVFs can cause substantial morbidity and potentially death through neurological deficits or intracranial hemorrhage. Symptoms, CVD, and venous drainage help distinguish benign from aggressive disease; the Borden and Cognard classifications describe relevant drainage patterns in NCS dAVFs. Initial conservative management is a viable option for benign, low-risk dAVFs, although close clinical and imaging follow-up may be indicated because CVD can develop in a small proportion. Definitive treatment is often recommended for complex, high-grade fistulas. An earlier meta-analysis reported CO of 82% after embolization, with PND, morbidity, and mortality rates of 4%, 3%, and 0%, respectively. Embolization, with or without ligation, does not always provide CO or durable cure. SRS is therefore often used after planned or unsuccessful embolization to achieve CO, relieve symptoms, and prevent possible later neurological complications, while recognizing that CO may be delayed. In arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), SRS has been associated with risk reductions of roughly 50% during the interval before CO and 90% once CO is achieved. Earlier SRS meta-analyses addressed CO but did not include additional studies updating CO rates or estimates for symptom improvement, symptom cure, hemorrhage after SRS, and PNDs. The present analysis found pooled CO of approximately 70%, symptom improvement of approximately 97%, symptom cure of approximately 80%, and PND and hemorrhage rates of approximately 1%. Hemorrhage after SRS for dAVFs appeared very low compared with AVM outcomes, without a significant latency period; however, this analysis lacked timing data relating CO to SRS. Longer follow-up in additional series may partly explain the higher CO estimate relative to previous reviews. Better target delineation combining digital subtraction angiography, thin-slice MRI/A, and CT may also have contributed, compared with earlier reliance mainly on angiography. Earlier studies identified location, CVD, and pre-SRS embolization as potentially prognostic. Pan et al reported CO of 70% for CS versus 59% for NCS dAVFs. Another study reported 100% for CS versus 40% for NCS dAVFs (P = .034). An earlier systematic review found a nonsignificant CS–NCS difference of 73% versus 58% (P = .27). The discussion attributes more favorable CO without versus with CVD to Hanakita et al (86% vs 47%) and Wang et al (66.7% vs 25%); Chen et al also reported a significant association between CVD and lower CO (75% vs 56%; P = .03). In this analysis, studies with more NCS dAVFs had significantly worse CO and symptom cure. Yang et al reported higher CO with embolization plus SRS than SRS alone (83% vs 67%), as did Oh et al (83% vs 54%). This analysis associated prior embolization with significantly better symptom cure, but found no effect on CO rates from CVD frequency or increasing dose beyond contemporary MPDs. Relief of symptoms caused by venous congestion is another SRS goal. Early series reported improvement in approximately half of patients, whereas newer series reported 90%-100%. A prior study reported symptom palliation of 100% for CS and 96% for NCS dAVFs, without a demonstrated association between location and symptom improvement. Earlier findings likewise did not show that Borden class or CVD correlated with symptom improvement or cure. In contrast, this analysis associated greater NCS representation and higher Borden grade with less symptom cure, but not less symptom improvement. Criteria for selecting patients for SRS remain incompletely defined; CVD, previous intracerebral hemorrhage, and NCS location likely matter for decisions. The pooled PND and hemorrhage rates after SRS were approximately 1% each. Reported PNDs included reduced visual acuity and hearing loss, both confined to earlier studies. The reviewed studies did not identify dAVF or patient features associated with either complication; this analysis nevertheless found more hemorrhage after SRS among patients with prior hemorrhage, while finding no examined predictor of PNDs. Table 2 presents the proposed SRS practice guidance. Observation with conservative care is a viable initial choice for CS and low-grade intracranial dAVFs. Definitive treatment is recommended for high-grade NCS dAVFs, including Borden types II and III, because of possible morbidity and mortality. It is also recommended for CS or low-risk NCS dAVFs when symptoms persist or progress after conservative care, given the low morbidity associated with SRS. Embolization is recommended first-line for high-grade and/or symptomatic dAVFs. SRS is recommended as adjuvant or salvage treatment when a complex fistula is unlikely to be obliterated by embolization alone, when hemorrhage preceded definitive treatment, or when embolization has not achieved CO and/or symptoms recur; this is especially relevant if ligation is infeasible or refused. Combining embolization and SRS is recommended when feasible for clinically aggressive or embolization-refractory fistulas to improve the likelihood of symptom cure. Embolization may shrink the fistula and make SRS safer, but may also obscure it on stereotactic targeting images. SRS is recommended if ligation or embolization is infeasible, given frequent CO and symptom relief with few adverse events. Patients should be counseled that CO can take time after SRS. Single-fraction SRS is recommended for definitive, adjuvant, or salvage treatment using contemporary MPDs of approximately 17-25 Gy, according to fistula size and surrounding normal-tissue tolerances. Planning should use catheter cerebral angiography and thin-slice MRI of 1 mm slice or less, particularly T1 sequences before and after gadolinium; CT is an alternative if MRI is infeasible. MRI is particularly recommended, when feasible, for targets near the brain stem, cochlea, or optic apparatus. If embolization precedes SRS, planning images should be obtained afterward to define the residual fistula. The target should generally contain only the fistula, excluding its feeding artery and draining vein. A 1-mm planning target volume expansion may be used when needed for setup uncertainty, depending on the technology. Follow-up should use MRI/A, or CT/A if MRI is infeasible, every 6 months to assess obliteration. If CT or MRI suggests CO, cerebral angiography is recommended for definitive confirmation. If confirmation by angiography cannot be performed, MRI/A or CT/CTA may establish CO with a high degree of confidence.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Every included study was retrospective. Differences in follow-up and patient attrition create substantial risk of bias in the pooled estimates. Because the analysis used study-level rather than individual-patient data, it could not adjust for Borden/Cognard type, target size, hemorrhage or symptoms before SRS, prior embolization or microsurgery, time between earlier treatments and SRS, CVD or leptomeningeal drainage, fistula location, or retrograde versus anterograde flow. Although angiography generally established CO, reliance on MRI or CT alone in some studies and differing follow-up periods may have biased that outcome. Differences across institutions and treatment eras in patient selection, planning, and follow-up contributed to significant heterogeneity in several pooled estimates. Too few series separated outcomes for SRS alone from SRS combined with embolization or surgery to permit comparison of CO or symptom relief between single-modality and multimodality treatment.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSION
document_sections.content: The authors consider SRS an effective and safe option for dAVFs: most treated patients achieve CO, and symptom palliation is strong. Treatment combined with embolization was associated with better symptom cure. Previous hemorrhage should be taken into account when discussing hemorrhage risk after SRS with patients.
